Caveblazers: A Brutal Roguelike That Makes You Love the PainIf you're a fan of punishing games that don't hold your hand, Caveblazers is a fantastic pick. It blends the level exploration of Spelunky with the chaotic, overwhelming horde combat of Risk of Rain into a fast-paced 2D action platformer.The Story & ConceptThe narrative is straightforward and sets up the action perfectly. You play an intrepid adventurer plumbing the depths of a newly discovered cave system rumored to hold "unimaginable power". Instead of deep lore, you get an abundance of weapons, magical items, orcs, and goblins looking to end your run instantly.Gameplay & MechanicsSeamless Combat: The flow between melee and ranged weapon switching feels incredibly tight. Running and gunning with the bow is highly satisfying, though using a controller is heavily recommended for the 8-directional aiming grid.Perks and Customization: Before dropping into the cave, you can pick specific Perks (like getting extra starting bombs or health items). Finding unique blessings and magic rings mid-run can completely change your playstyle.High RNG Dependence: Runs live and die by RNG. You can either get a legendary combo that makes you unstoppable, or mistakenly drink an unknown potion that sets you on fire and ruins everything.Pros & ConsPROS:Charming Pixel Art: The animation cycles are surprisingly fluid, and the particle and arrow effects look great on screen.Tight Platforming: Movement and ledge grabbing feel incredibly responsive, which is critical during tight combat situations.Deep Progression: Dying never feels entirely useless as you constantly unlock new items, challenges, and cosmetic hats for future attempts.CONS:Boss Balancing: Some boss stages feel explicitly designed against melee-heavy builds, almost forcing you to rely strictly on ranged damage.Final VerdictCaveblazers fully deserves its "Very Positive" status on Steam. It’s tough, sometimes unfair, but addictive enough to keep you saying "just one more run".

I love this game to bits. I remember playing this game for the first time years ago on my friend's crappy HP computer, because this was the only game it could really run. I've been playing Caveblazers for maybe over a decade on multiple different platforms, and have just never gotten tired of it. The simplicity of the items, and how you can synergize weapons and abilities to get some crazy runs, and how easy it is to just get back into it. 

I do think there are some small balance issues, but not enough to dampen the experience. Ranged builds are much stronger than melee builds for the simple reason of not needing to be in the enemy's face to defeat them.

The logbook, the different classes, the items, and the feeling of discovery locked behind genuinely frustrating rooms - It's just incredible that this game is able to tickle all the videogame buttons in my head. 

I'll be honest, I'm not great at it; I die often, and sometimes have to stop playing because of the aforementioned frustrating rooms. 

One of the other things about this game is the music. Now, they aren't songs I'd listen to outside the game, but they are all a masterclass of tone setting and ambience. The intro song is iconic for me, and makes me happy.

If the developer ever reads this, I just want to thank you for your work. I think it is criminally underrated and deserves more love. 

- Also, if you're doing more on the game, it'd be cool if you could add a feature to custom mode where you can create a crazy build. Or maybe an infinite mode. I think it would be really funny to have four super rebound emblems and a ton of exploding arrows and crash the game :)

Caveblazers, developed by Deadpan Games and published by Yogscast Games, is a demanding 2D roguelike platformer that thrives on unpredictability, mechanical precision, and relentless escalation. Set within a sprawling, monster-infested cave system, the game invites players to descend ever deeper in search of treasure and glory, fully aware that each run may end abruptly in disaster. Rather than leaning on elaborate storytelling or cinematic presentation, it builds its identity around tight gameplay systems and procedural variety, creating an experience that rewards persistence and skill in equal measure.

At the heart of Caveblazers lies its procedurally generated structure. Every descent into the cavern reshuffles level layouts, enemy placements, loot drops, and environmental hazards, ensuring that no two runs are identical. Platforms crumble unexpectedly, traps lie in wait, and enemies often collide with one another as much as with the player. This systemic unpredictability creates a living ecosystem inside the cave, where chaos can either hinder or help depending on how well the player adapts. It encourages awareness of surroundings at all times, as danger can emerge from above, below, or off-screen without warning.

Combat plays a central role in maintaining the game’s intensity. Weapons range from basic melee arms like swords and axes to bows, magical staves, and exotic artifacts that alter combat behavior dramatically. Each weapon carries its own attack rhythm, range, and recoil properties, making mastery of timing essential. Movement is deliberately weighty but responsive, forcing players to commit to jumps and swings rather than button-mashing through encounters. Enemies are varied and often aggressive, from small nuisance creatures to imposing minibosses that demand patience and pattern recognition. Boss encounters punctuate progression through the cave, serving as climactic tests of reflexes and preparation.

One of the most distinctive mechanics involves potions and blessings, many of which have randomized or hidden effects. Drinking an unidentified potion could grant powerful regeneration—or inflict poison and chaos. This risk-reward dynamic injects tension into decision-making, especially when resources are scarce. Blessings earned through leveling add another layer of customization, allowing players to tailor builds around offensive boosts, defensive resilience, mobility enhancements, or situational perks. Over time, accumulated experience unlocks additional gear and options for future runs, creating a satisfying meta-progression system that softens the sting of inevitable defeat.

Visually, Caveblazers embraces a pixel-art aesthetic that recalls classic 16-bit platformers while incorporating modern lighting and particle effects. The caves are moody and atmospheric, with shifting color palettes that differentiate biomes as players descend further underground. Though the art style is simple, it effectively communicates enemy silhouettes and environmental hazards, which is crucial during frantic combat sequences. The soundtrack complements the action with energetic tracks that heighten tension without overwhelming the player’s focus.

Difficulty is both a defining strength and a potential barrier. Caveblazers is unapologetically punishing, with permadeath resetting immediate progress and forcing players back to the beginning. Encounters can spiral out of control quickly, particularly when environmental hazards intersect with enemy swarms. For players who relish the challenge of mastering complex systems through repetition and incremental improvement, this creates a deeply addictive loop. However, those less inclined toward trial-and-error design may find the steep learning curve intimidating.

Despite its straightforward premise—venture into a cave and survive—the game achieves impressive depth through the interplay of systems. Environmental physics, enemy AI interactions, randomized loot, and player upgrades combine to create emergent moments that feel unscripted and personal. A run might be defined by a perfectly timed potion gamble, a miraculous last-second dodge, or an unexpected chain reaction between enemies and traps. These dynamic events ensure that even failure feels like part of an evolving story shaped by player choices.

Ultimately, Caveblazers stands as a robust example of modern roguelike platforming done with precision and focus. It prioritizes mechanical clarity, replayability, and escalating challenge over narrative complexity, offering a pure test of skill and adaptability. For players who appreciate tightly tuned combat, procedural unpredictability, and the satisfaction of incremental mastery, it delivers a compelling and long-lasting experience. While its unforgiving nature may not appeal to everyone, those willing to embrace its demanding design will find a richly layered descent into danger that remains engaging run after run.

Caveblazers — динамичный платформер с элементами "рогалика" в фэнтезийном мире. Уровни генерируются случайно, предлагая уникальные предметы, оружие и экипировку.

Сюжет разворачивается вокруг пещеры с "невероятной силой". Вы играете за исследователя, сталкиваясь с новыми зонами, монстрами и боссами.

Персонажи обладают продвинутым ИИ: дружелюбные следуют за вами, а враждебные находят даже при попытке спрятаться.

Игра сочетает элементы платформера и "рогалика": перманентная смерть, рандомизированные зелья, система инвентаря и множество улучшений.

Каждый день предлагает уникальное испытание с ограниченными стартовыми предметами.

Боссы требуют особого подхода, занимая весь экран.

Кастомизация включает широкий выбор одежды и аксессуаров.

Боевая система динамична и включает кровавые эффекты.

Для опытных игроков доступны испытания с ценными наградами.

Had a lot of potential and can be fun in brief instances but falls into the same trap as far, far to many mediocre indie tiles by trying to difficulty gate it's limited content to extend playtime. Like many indie procedurally generated "rogue likes", it isn't novel, interesting or fun enough to warrant any kind of progression system or the time it demands to enjoy all that it has to offer.

Only being able to shoot in 8 directions is an either stupid or incompetent design choice in a game that goes out of it's way to demand hyper reflexes for the sake of arbitrary difficulty. Combat in general feels very underdeveloped as ranged attack builds (even if hindered by poor targeting) are superior because at least you can keep your distance from the bad combat system.

In summary, it's a procedurally generated, lo-fi, side-scrolling action game that is more difficult then it deserves to be with responsive controls, very little depth, unfulfilling progression systems, sometimes cheap damage/deaths and everything in it is mediocre (nothing is particularly novel or exceptionally well done). Worth a dollar. Not 10.
